vignette:
Ravi Patel, a 44-year-old South Asian man who worked as a chef, came to treatment after years of trying to keep himself busy enough not to think. He had come to the United States as a refugee after violence in his home country, and the account he gave of the event that still anchored his distress was fixed around a single chaotic day when people were running, shouting, and trying to get to safety while he was trapped in the midst of it. He spoke carefully about that time, often stopping short of details, saying that he could not seem to put the frightening event into words. What he could describe was the sensory outline: the confusion of bodies moving past him, the sight of people with visible injuries and wounds, the sudden appearance of uniforms and weapons that made the danger feel immediate again, and the sirens that followed afterward. Even now, if he heard talk about accidents or saw an ambulance pass outside the restaurant where he worked, his attention would snap toward it before he could stop himself. The same happened if a customer at the counter mentioned a crash or an injury on the news. Ravi would go quiet, stare down at his hands, and wait for the wave of discomfort to pass.

In the months after he resettled, he found himself carrying the event in fragments rather than a clear story. Sometimes he could recall what happened, but it felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. At other times, especially when he allowed himself to think about those he had lost, the memory came with overwhelming grief that left him standing in the kitchen for a long time, unable to resume chopping or plating. He said he had never forgiven himself for not doing more to stop what happened, even though he also knew, rationally, that he had been one person in a situation that was already beyond control. Still, he believed he should have acted differently. He also carried a deep sense of guilt for surviving when others did not. That belief was not abstract for him; it surfaced most sharply on anniversaries, when he would picture people who had not made it out and feel that his own life had been spared at their expense. He described himself as permanently changed for the worse, someone who once moved through the world more easily and now felt “marked” in a way others could not see.

Over time, Ravi’s days became organized around staying prepared. He was superalert and watchful wherever he went, scanning the room before sitting down, checking who was near the door, and always identifying escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere. In public places, especially open or exposed spaces, he felt vulnerable and chose seats against walls or near exits. He avoided military and police uniforms whenever possible, crossing the street or lowering his gaze if he saw them in his neighborhood. He noticed that he was also increasingly compliant when he felt threatened, a habit he recognized in himself without liking it. In difficult interactions, including with customers or supervisors, he would nod quickly, agree too readily, and try to smooth things over before anyone became upset. He described this as a kind of reflex, something that happened before he had time to decide.

At work, these habits quietly shaped his life. As a chef, he spent long hours in a busy kitchen where people moved quickly, talked over one another, and sometimes arrived with injuries from knives or hot pans. If a server walked through with a bandaged hand or if he caught sight of a fresh wound, he felt a jolt of unease and had to look away. Fire doors, loading areas, and the open stretch of parking lot behind the restaurant all made him uneasy because they felt exposed. He preferred to remain near the prep line or stove, where there were barriers and clear sightlines, and he had developed the habit of mentally mapping how he would get out if something went wrong. His concentration had become unreliable in these moments; while reading orders or organizing ingredients, his mind would drift to scanning the room or checking the door, and he would have to ask for instructions to be repeated. Although he continued to work, he was increasingly tired by the effort of staying alert.

Ravi finally sought help when the strain of keeping these routines intact began to leave him isolated and exhausted. He had been turning down social invitations because restaurants, sidewalks, and even parking lots felt too open, and because talk of accidents or seeing injury could still throw him off balance. He wanted relief from the constant watchfulness and the grief that could rise so suddenly when the memory surfaced. More than anything, he was afraid that the version of himself he had become was permanent, that survival had left him damaged in a way that would never fully let him return to the man he had been.
